displayQuote: The way to make a million dollars is to start a religion

meta.title: Who really said "The way to make a million dollars is to start a religion"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: L. Ron Hubbard, on the testimony of several science-fiction contemporaries in the 1940s — including a sworn affidavit from Sam Moskowitz about a Newark meeting in November 1948. No recording or manuscript exists, and Scientology disputes it. Verified by witnesses, not by document.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The way to make a million dollars is to start a religion'?
meta.ogDescription: Hubbard almost certainly said something like it — four separate witnesses across the 1940s, one under oath. But there is no recording, no manuscript, and no two witnesses agree on the words.

answer.label: Hubbard — attested by witnesses, not by any document
answer.authorDates: 1911–1986 · pulp science-fiction writer, founder of Dianetics and Scientology
answer.sourceLine: This is an unusual case, and worth stating precisely: the remark is well attested and undocumented at the same time. At least four people who knew Hubbard in the 1940s independently recalled him saying a version of it — the fullest account is Sam Moskowitz, who ran the Eastern Science Fiction Association and later swore an affidavit about a meeting in Newark on 7 November 1948. But there is no recording, no manuscript and no contemporaneous note, no two witnesses give the same words, and the Church of Scientology disputes the whole thing, producing two attendees who swore he said no such thing. Believe it or not on the strength of the testimony; there is no document to settle it.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: You don't get rich writing science fiction. If you want to get rich, you start a religion.
trail: Sam Moskowitz is the anchor. A well-known science-fiction historian and the director of the Eastern Science Fiction Association, he said Hubbard gave this answer to a question about making money from writing at a meeting in Newark, New Jersey. He repeated the story for decades and eventually set it down in a signed affidavit the collected accounts ↗.

He was not the only one. The publisher Lloyd Arthur Eshbach recalled Hubbard saying ‘I’d like to start a religion. That’s where the money is’ and printed it in his 1983 memoir Over My Shoulder. The editor Sam Merwin recalled a similar remark from around December 1946, and Neison Himmel, who briefly shared rooms with Hubbard in Pasadena in the autumn of 1945, told an interviewer that Hubbard often said the easiest way to make money would be to start a religion. Those two accounts appear in Russell Miller’s Bare-Faced Messiah (1987).

Moskowitz was also interviewed about Hubbard by the US Food and Drug Administration, whose Scientology investigation files — the E-meter case — have since been declassified and put online. We have located the released collection but not the individual interview memo, so we do not quote from it and we do not give it a page reference the released FDA files ↗.

The Church of Scientology denies it flatly, and its objections are specific rather than hand-waving: two other attendees of the Newark meeting, David A. Kyle and Jay Kay Klein, swore Hubbard said nothing of the kind, and the surviving minutes of that meeting summarise his remarks without any such line the Church’s case ↗.

What we could not establish: which wording, if any, Hubbard actually used. The versions range from ‘start a religion’ to ‘start a cult’, and the round ‘million dollars’ of the popular form appears in some retellings and not others.
source.excerptNote: Moskowitz's wording, as given in his affidavit. It is worth seeing how far it is from the polished aphorism people quote: it is an answer to a question about the pulp rates, from a man who was at that moment being paid roughly a penny a word. The version everyone knows has been tidied into an epigram.

source.rightsNote: We give no rights status, because there is no first publication to hang one on: the sentence exists only in other people’s recollections, each of which carries its own copyright. Moskowitz’s affidavit and Eshbach’s 1983 memoir belong to their authors and estates; the FDA interview memo, as a US government record, is not protected. Hubbard died in 1986 and his own writings are in copyright until 2056 in the UK and EU, and are policed unusually vigorously — but a sentence he is reported to have said in conversation is not a work of his. Quote it with attribution, as reported speech, and name the witness. This is not legal advice.

author.name: L. Ron Hubbard
author.heading: About L. Ron Hubbard
author.metaLine: 1911–1986 · pulp science-fiction writer, founder of Dianetics and Scientology
author.bio: L. Ron Hubbard (1911–1986) was a prolific and fast pulp writer — westerns, adventure, science fiction — before publishing Dianetics in 1950 and founding the Church of Scientology in 1953. The remark on this page is quoted so often because of what happened next, and that is also the reason to handle it carefully: a line that sounds like a confession of intent is exactly the kind of thing memory improves over forty years. Several people who knew him in the pulp years recalled him saying it; the Church has contested it for as long as it has circulated, and Hubbard himself is not recorded as being asked about it.

cite.sourceCitation: Reported speech. No recording or manuscript exists; disputed by the Church of Scientology.

misattribution.heading: How good is the evidence?
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is offered as the author, so this is not a misattribution question. It is an evidence question: how much weight can several old memories carry when there is no document behind them?

items.why: Moskowitz, Eshbach, Merwin and Himmel were not collaborating, and their recollections span 1945 to 1949 in three different cities. Independent convergence on the same idea is real evidence, even when the wording differs.

items.who: One of them swore to it
items.why: Moskowitz put his account in a signed affidavit rather than an anecdote, which raises the cost of being wrong — and he was a serious historian of the field, not a hostile stranger.
Minutes of the Newark meeting survive and summarise Hubbard’s remarks without it. Minutes are selective, but this is a genuine hole in the strongest account the Church’s case ↗.

David A. Kyle and Jay Kay Klein, both present, stated that Hubbard said nothing of the kind. Sworn statements on both sides is exactly the situation a document would resolve, and there is no document.

‘You don’t get rich writing science fiction — if you want to get rich, you start a religion.’ ‘I’d like to start a religion. That’s where the money is.’ ‘The easiest way to make money would be to start a religion.’ The polished million-dollar version on this page is the one that circulates and the one no witness actually reports.
A similar line about founding a religion for profit is occasionally attached to Orwell or to Mark Twain. Neither has a source; the Hubbard version is the only one with named witnesses attached.

misattribution.truthLine: Attested but undocumented. Several people who knew Hubbard in the 1940s recalled him saying a version of it, one of them under oath — but there is no recording, no manuscript, no agreed wording, and the Church of Scientology contests it with sworn statements of its own the accounts ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is quoted as a smoking gun: proof that the whole thing was a business plan announced in advance. That is why the evidential standard matters more here than on almost any other quotation we handle — the line is doing work that only a document could really justify.

Read without that freight, it is also just a very good joke about being paid a penny a word. Hubbard was one of the fastest pulp writers alive and still not rich, and the room he supposedly said it in was full of people in exactly the same position.
detailsBody: Autumn 1945, Pasadena: Neison Himmel, briefly Hubbard's roommate, recalls him saying the easiest way to make money would be to start a religion. Interviewed in 1986 for Bare-Faced Messiah.
December 1946: the editor Sam Merwin recalls a similar remark, also recorded in Bare-Faced Messiah.

7 November 1948, Newark: the Eastern Science Fiction Association meeting at the heart of the dispute. Sam Moskowitz's account; two other attendees later swore it did not happen. A date of 11 November also circulates.
1949: the publisher Lloyd Arthur Eshbach recalls 'I'd like to start a religion. That's where the money is', printed in his 1983 memoir Over My Shoulder.
1950: Dianetics is published. 1953: the Church of Scientology is founded.
1978-80: the saying reaches a mass audience through the Los Angeles Times and Reader's Digest, by which point the wording has hardened into the epigram.
context.pull: Four witnesses, one affidavit, no document. That is a real category — and it is not the same as proof.
